signals.title: Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
signals.excerpt:
Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
# GPT-6.1 Terra
## Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale
We’re introducing **GPT-6.1 Terra**, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.
## From visual understanding to action
We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on **Agents’ Last Exam,** a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a \~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks **over three times faster** than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
On **MMMU-Pro**, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.
**OSWorld 2.1** tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.
## A significant step up on factuality and coding
This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. **Terminal-Bench 4.0** tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.
**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1** tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.
## Safety and alignment
As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.
GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).
## Pricing and availability
Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as `gpt-6.1-terra`.
Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

signals.title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
# Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK

by Prabhakar Chandrasekaran and Siddhant Sahu on 26 OCT 2026 in Advanced (300), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Technical How-to Permalink Share

This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated.

It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question, and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen.

Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works.

...

From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation. The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository, so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.

signals.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary.

Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs:

- Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation.
- Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume.
- Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together.

This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook.

...

## Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization

In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression.

The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.

This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path.

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |

Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming alone

...

## Conclusion

Across the full GSM8K evaluation, the three optimizations increased decode throughput by 42.5%, reduced mean end-to-end latency by 24.5%, and produced no statistically detectable accuracy change. Their mechanisms do not overlap: Humming and the FP8 LM head reduce the cost of each step, while MTP reduces the number of steps, so the techniques can be combined.

Stacking, however, is not automatic. Each optimization worked independently, but enabling all three required the draft model to share the full LM-head module. Otherwise, the system silently degrades to a configuration slower than the unoptimized baseline. During deployment, validate that every optimization is active at startup; this is more reliable than inferring configuration state from later performance numbers.

# Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence

OCT 27, 2026

Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3, our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face, our Playground, and the Liquid AI API. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

## Highlights

- More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform our previous LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
- Every modality, one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base. 
- Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision. 
- New flagship in-house vision and audio encoders.
- 256K context window for the text model.
- Made to be specialized: every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

LFM3 instances are ideal candidates for specialized intelligence. Fine-tune them on your own data, and deploy them where your application runs. Enjoy the article.

signals.title: Sulci 1.0: a context-aware semantic cache for agents, and the number most caches don’t publish - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Sulci 1.0: a context-aware semantic cache for agents, and the number most caches don’t publish - DEV Community
Posted on Oct 27
# Sulci 1.0: a context-aware semantic cache for agents, and the number most caches don’t publish
### Stable library, hosted tier generally available, every benchmark figure reproducible from the public repo
Today Sulci is 1.0, and the hosted tier is generally available.
Sulci is an open-source, context-aware semantic cache for LLM apps and AI agents. When a new query *means* the same thing as a past one, you get the cached answer instead of another model call, even when the words are different. It's Apache 2.0, it runs on infrastructure you already have, and it's three lines around an existing call.
## Why agents need this
We instrumented an agent workload: 50 sessions, 200 LLM dispatches each, the ReAct-ish mix you get when a tool-using agent works a task.
* With a cold, empty cache, **33.4%**`[30.00–35.00%]` of dispatches could be served from cache.
* Warm, within the same session, **99.7%**`[99.69–99.81%]`.
* The **median session sent 2 of its 200 dispatches** to the model. The p95 session sent 53 `[46–64]`, mostly cold ones, and we publish that too.
None of this means agents are broken. Loops re-derive the same intermediate facts, planners re-summarise the same context at every step, retries re-ask the failing question slightly rephrased. The dispatch stream is mostly near duplicates, and the bill scales with the redundancy, not with the work.
## The number most caches don't publish
A semantic cache has one failure people remember: a confident wrong answer, served because two questions looked alike. A cache tuned only for hit rate reaches 100% by answering everything.
So our benchmark corpus is built so that **39% of test queries have no correct answer cached**, and we publish what the cache does with them. Four seeded draws, threshold 0.85, the shipped MiniLM embedder:
||measured|range across draws|
|Repeat questions served from cache|**99.9%**|`[99.85–99.95%]`|
|Correctly declined when it has no answer|**98.9%**|`[98.15–99.38%]`|
|Of cache hits, share that are correct|**93.8%**|`[92.13–94.69%]`|
|Cache hit, p50|**87ms**|`[86.956–87.729ms]`, quiet M-series machine|
87ms is almost entirely the embedding, not the lookup, and it depends on your hardware. Measure it on yours.
Reproduce one draw in a clone of the repo (the benchmark isn't in the PyPI package):
```
git clone https://github.com/sulci-io/sulci-oss && cd sulci-oss
pip install -e ".[sqlite]"
python benchmark/run.py --use-sulci --fresh --no-sweep --agent --seed 1 --out /tmp/sulci-bench
```
Then `--seed 2`, `3` and `42`. If you get something different, open an issue with your seed and your machine.
## How you use it
```
pip install "sulci[sqlite]"
```
```
from sulci import Cache

cache = Cache(backend="sqlite", threshold=0.85)

response, similarity, context_depth = cache.get("How do I rotate an API key?")
if response is None:
    response = call_your_model(...)
    cache.set("How do I rotate an API key?", response)
```
`threshold=` can be overridden on each call, so a strict path and a loose path can share one cache.
## It remembers the conversation
Sulci is context-aware. Pass a `session\_id` and each lookup blends the current query with the conversation's recent turns: 70% the query, 30% a decaying history. "How do I fix it?" after a Docker crash and "How do I fix it?" after a billing error search with two different vectors.
We're careful about what that does and doesn't promise. Blending changes where a follow-up searches; it doesn't make a stored follow-up belong to one conversation. On our corpus, on MiniLM, it didn't measurably improve resolution accuracy (more below). So the hosted tier adds two guards:
* Blended lookups have to clear a stricter bar (0.80, against 0.65 for plain lookups).
* A follow-up that only makes sense inside its conversation is **never stored as a shared answer**. The API says so in its response: `stored: false, reason: "context\_dependent"`.
It's on by default there. In the library you opt in with `context\_window` and a `session\_id`, and tune `query\_weight`, `context\_decay` and `context\_threshold` yourself.
## Adopt it without rewriting anything
Whatever your agent stack looks like, there's a door that costs a line or less:
|You have|You add|
|LangChain or LangGraph|`set\_llm\_cache(SulciCache(backend="sqlite"))`: one line, every LLM call and graph node cached|
|LlamaIndex|wrap your LLM in `SulciCacheLLM` and pass `session\_id=`|
|LiteLLM|`from sulci.integrations.litellm import install` and call it; LiteLLM's 100+ providers are now cached|
|Any OpenAI or Anthropic client, in any language|`pip install "sulci[proxy]"`, run `sulci-proxy` and set `OPENAI\_BASE\_URL` / `ANTHROPIC\_BASE\_URL`. **No code change.** Hits come back with `x-sulci-cache: hit`|
|An agent that can't import Python|`pip install "sulci[mcp]"` for `sulci-mcp`, an MCP server (stdio, SSE or streamable HTTP, with a read-only mode)|
|TypeScript, Go, Java…|`npm install @sulci/sulci`, or the HTTPS API|
The same `session\_id` carries through the library, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, the proxy (as an `x-sulci-session-id` header), the MCP server, the TypeScript client and the HTTP API. Storage is SQLite to start, then Chroma, Qdrant, FAISS, Redis (plain Redis, no modules) or Milvus, with the same three lines.
## What 1.0 means
The library is declared stable. From 1.0.0, Semantic Versioning holds for the public API in `docs/API-SURFACE.md`: no breaking change within 1.x, additions in minor releases, fixes in patch releases.
## The hosted tier is generally available
Keep your self-hosted backend and pass an API key, and the free dashboard shows hit rates and cost saved per deployment. Only a fixed allowlist of eight operational fields is sent. Your queries, responses and embeddings stay where they are.
Or let us host the cache: `Cache(backend="sulci", api\_key="sk-sulci-...")`. In that mode your query text and cached responses do reach us, because that's what hosting the cache means. The privacy policy spells out both modes.
Pro and Business are generally available — self-serve signup with a 14-day or 50k-request trial, and a one-parameter upgrade from self-hosted. OSS-Connect (10,000 managed requests a month, no card) stays free. Pro is $29/month and Business $149/month. Details at https://sulci.io/pricing.
## What we're deliberately not claiming
* **No cost-per-query figure and no speedup multiple.** Both depend on your model, your token counts and how repetitive your traffic is, and no benchmark of ours predicts that. https://sulci.io/roi does the arithmetic with your numbers instead of ours.
* **No context-aware accuracy delta.** Sulci blends exponentially decayed prior turns into the lookup vector, and it ships. On the shipped embedder, on our corpus, it showed no measurable gain in resolution accuracy: MiniLM already answers most conversational follow-ups statelessly. Earlier numbers showing a large gain were measured against a TF-IDF baseline with far more headroom. We withdrew them rather than shrinking them.
## Try it
* GitHub: https://github.com/sulci-io/sulci-oss
* Docs and a live in-browser demo (no signup): https://sulci.io/demo
* PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/sulci/
* Pricing: https://sulci.io/pricing
Apache 2.0. A U.S. patent application covering aspects of context-aware semantic caching is pending (No. 64/018,452); it is currently assigned to Kathiravan Sengodan. The Apache-2.0 patent grant in the LICENSE file applies to the open-source contribution as licensed thereunder.

signals.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
signals.excerpt:
Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
* Article
* Open access
* Published: 26 October 2026
# Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
* Enmiao Feng 1,
* Gaike Wang 2,
* Pengfei Li 1,
* Yinuo Wang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-3927-0742 3 &
* …
* Shan Huang 4
## Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained *entirely offline*, without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated *distribution* over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from \\(71.3\\%\\) (FCFS) and \\(84.1\\%\\) (learning-to-rank) to \\(90.4\\%\\), cuts P99 TTFT by up to \\(3.3\\times \\), and reduces recompute/eviction events below \\(1\\%\\), approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

# KV Cache砍掉99%，单卡吞吐飙6倍，港科CMU联手岩山科技开源新模型

 一水 2026-10-26 14:45:25 来源：量子位 

一张卡，512路长推理同时跑

> 允中 发自 凹非寺
> 
> 量子位 | 公众号 QbitAI

谷歌今年的一篇论文，愣是把存储芯片巨头的股价都给整出动静了。

论文里提到， KV Cache至少能压缩6倍。

要知道，大模型推理越来越吃内存，KV Cache又是其中一笔不小的开销。

现在谷歌突然把它压下去这么多，美光等存储芯片巨头的股价随之下跌。

结果才过去几个月，又有人对KV Cache下了更狠的一刀。

这次连压缩都不满足了。

上下文从4K一路涨到256K，KV Cache占用愣是没变。

在256K上下文下，始终固定在72MiB。相比源模型，KV Cache直接减少 99.1%。

更夸张的是，一张80GB显卡同时跑512路长推理，输出吞吐达到12124 tokens/s，是源模型的6.42倍。

而且推理能力也基本保住了，AIME 2024—2026平均一次通过率达到82.9%，而参评的有界状态模型即便做到14B，最好也只有18.8%。

这就是岩山科技旗下岩芯矩阵联合港科大、CMU等高校刚刚发布并开源的

signals.excerpt: Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs.

By

## What does the AKV API look like?

The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. `drop_message` maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. `reposition` lists the indices after which positions get compacted.

A `CachePolicy` builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A `CacheTool` lets the model call `drop_context` itself.

signals.title: Cerebras trillion-parameter model deployment — Grafy News
signals.excerpt:
Grafy News Desk Oct 25, 2026 6 min read

Cerebras has published a detailed account of how it runs multi-trillion-parameter models across dozens of wafer-scale processors, describing a pipeline in which model weights stay on chip and only activations travel between wafers at roughly two microseconds per hop. It matters because the post turns an abstract claim about frontier-scale inference into a specific architecture, with trade-offs developers can inspect and test.

...

A single WSE-3T wafer provides 44 GB of on-chip memory, according to Cerebras, while trillion-parameter models need terabytes for their weights alone. The answer is to spread the model across many wafers rather than squeeze it into one.

The worked example is Kimi K3, described as an open-source model with about 3 trillion parameters, 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers. Cerebras assumes 4-bit weight quantization, in the manner of the Hugging Face implementation, an 8-bit KV cache, and a 256k assumed average request size.

On those assumptions, each of the model's 93 layers comes to roughly 16 GB. Because a layer fits comfortably inside 44 GB, Cerebras can keep whole layers resident on a chip instead of splitting them across wafers.

...

## How do the wafers pass work between them?

Cerebras executes models as a pipeline. Its compiler maps model layers across regions of wafers, and the runtime maps the path tokens travel between them. Only activations cross between wafers, over RDMA over Ethernet, at roughly two microseconds per hop; weights generally do not move at all.

The assembly-line analogy in the post: wafer 1 runs layers 1–2 and sends activations to wafer 2, which runs layers 3–4 and passes results to wafer 3, until the last wafer produces the next token. Cerebras says production deployments use much finer-grained stages than the illustration.

...

The example is not a toy model. As described in Cerebras's post, Kimi K3 scores 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, against 88.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 91.2% on BrowseComp, against 90.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Open-weight models in the multi-trillion-parameter class are becoming servable at high token rates, and the architecture described here is a plausible reason why.

The caveat matters just as much. Cerebras notes that performance comparisons rest on third-party benchmarking or internal testing, and that observed speed improvements versus GPU-based systems may vary with workload, configuration, date and models tested. The method also scales: calculate memory for weights and request state, distribute across wafers, connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer adds compute and on-chip memory, allowing models larger than any single chip.

signals.title: Microsoft Open-Sources Agensh: A Multi-Agent Harness for 1,024 Agents - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
# Microsoft Open-Sources Agensh: A Multi-Agent Harness for 1,024 Agents

By

Asif Razzaq

October 24, 2026

Microsoft Research has open-sourced Agensh, a decentralized harness for large teams of coding agents. The Agensh multi-agent harness removes the central orchestrator that most agent frameworks depend on. Every worker picks its own sub-task, shares findings and merges code into a common Git repo. On ProgramBench, the team scaled the setup from 1 agent to 1,024 agents.

...

## How does the Agensh cooperation loop work?

Each worker runs the same 5-step loop, concurrently and asynchronously:

1. Gather context: read the goal, peer progress, messages and findings.
2. Claim a sub-task: post a CLAIM, then settle overlaps by direct message.
3. Take action: work locally with tools and post useful findings early.
4. Verify results: check the work against the sub-task’s acceptance criteria.
5. Merge progress: merge into the shared repo, post an update, then repeat.

Three services connect the workers. Gitea hosts the shared workspace, with branches, PRs and merge conflicts. Mattermost carries a team channel plus direct messages for urgent collisions. A shared context board, adapted from DeLM, stores typed notes: OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM and PATCH_SUMMARY.

The loop lives in the prompt, not in runtime code. Every worker gets the same prompt except its ID. Agensh sits on top of a single-agent harness. The experiments used GitHub Copilot CLI. The research paper states thin adapters can connect other harnesses, such as Claude Code.
